title: How AI Builds Cancer Drugs From Scratch | Aridni Shah, Immunito AI
description:
What if the biggest bottleneck in AI antibody discovery was never AlphaFold's problem to solve at all? Dr. Aridni Shah of Immunito AI sat down with host Akshay Datt to explain how her team builds antibodies from a target's shape alone, compressing a process that used to take animals a year and a half into hours. 
 Dr. Aridni Shah left academic structural biology, after a PhD at NCBS-TIFR studying honeybee brains, when she hit the wall every antibody researcher knows: custom antibody generation can take a year to eighteen months with no guarantee of success. That bottleneck became the founding insight behind Immunito AI, the Bengaluru TechBio company she co-founded with Trisha Chatterjee in 2020. Instead of injecting animals and waiting, Immunito AI uses generative AI to design antibodies atom by atom, directly from a target protein's shape, a technique the company built before AlphaFold existed. Across four internal preclinical oncology and autoimmune programmes, and licensing economics that can rival Merck's $30 billion Keytruda, the company is testing whether Indian deep tech can originate novel biologics instead of just manufacturing generics. In this conversation, Aridni walks host Akshay Datt through AI antibody discovery and why Indian venture capital still struggles to underwrite biotech risk. 
 👉How Immunito AI's AbInitio platform designs antibody sequences and 3D structures simultaneously from a target protein's shape, without animal immunization. 
 👉Why Aridni Shah's PhD research on honeybee time memory exposed the yearlong bottleneck in traditional antibody discovery that led her to found Immunito AI. 
 👉What makes AlphaFold different from Immunito AI's AbInitio, and why protein folding prediction alone cannot design a new antibody from scratch. 
 👉How a single preclinical antibody licensing deal can carry a $10 to $50 million upfront fee and $200 to $500 million in milestones, similar to how Merck's Keytruda scaled to $30 billion in annual sales. 
 👉Why Indian venture capital funds still struggle to underwrite biotech and drug discovery risk compared to US funds like a16z.

title: Ajay Jain (SilverX) on How To Pitch A VC

title: Financing Electric Trucks and Buses in India | Manav Bansal, Drivn
description:
An electric intercity bus costs ₹1.5 crore, which is exactly why almost nobody in India was financing them. Manav Bansal left a $2.5 billion investment mandate to build Drivn, and his answer to commercial EV leasing India starts with a structuring decision most founders never consider. 
 A civil engineer turned private equity investor, Manav Bansal spent close to three decades pricing infrastructure risk, ran two funds that lost money on zero investments, and oversaw a $2.5 billion India book at British International Investment before founding his first company at the back end of that career. Drivn buys electric intercity buses and 55 tonne trucks, owns them outright, and leases them to fleet operators, removing the upfront barrier that has kept India's heaviest and most polluting vehicles running on diesel. He explains why Drivn deliberately structured itself as an AssetCo rather than an NBFC to unlock cheap asset backed debt, how an electric bus runs at ₹35 a kilometre against ₹50 for diesel even after battery amortisation, and why the fear of dilution is overrated, all of which he unpacked in this conversation with host Akshay Datt. With India's first electric truck financing incentives barely moving on the ground, the electrification question has become a financing question.

title: Inside India's Gaming & Microdrama Boom | Salone Sehgal (Lumikai)
description:
India's gaming market crossed $14 billion this year - and it happened right after the real money gaming ban wiped out $2 billion of it overnight. Salone Sehgal, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Lumikai, has been building India's first dedicated gaming and interactive media VC fund since 2020, and every investor she pitched back then said the same thing: Indians will never pay for digital content. 
 After twelve years in Europe and $10 billion in M&A deals at Morgan Stanley, Salone built a London gaming studio, and wound it down so cleanly that her own seed investors hired her. Puma India went on to cross ₹2,000 crore in revenue, ahead of Nike and Adidas combined in India. Then, after nearly two decades in the industry, Abhishek chose to start again.

 Every general purpose technology gets invented once and scaled somewhere else. Germany invented the printing press. Britain built an industry on it. America turned that industry into an economy. Piyush Shah, Co-founder of InMobi and Glance, thinks the same pattern is repeating with AI right now, and he's convinced most founders are drawing the wrong lesson from it.
 On this episode of the Prime Venture Partners Podcast, Amit Somani sits down with Piyush to make the case that copying America's invention-first approach or China's industrialisation-first approach would be the wrong move for India entirely. Instead, Piyush lays out what he believes India's real opportunity looks like: not the smartest AI for the world's most sophisticated users, but AI that raises the floor for a billion people who've never had access to a tutor, a doctor, or a financial advisor in their life.
 The conversation doesn't stop at strategy. Piyush and Amit get into why consumer AI has a cost problem nobody's fully solved (he calls it inference CAC), why distribution remains the real moat even in an AI-native world, and why "purpose" might be the one advantage that's genuinely hard to copy. Piyush also opens up about how InMobi and Glance have rebuilt themselves around AI internally, and how AI has changed the way he runs his own life, from an 18-year-old AI-native chief of staff to using AI to understand his family's health reports.
 If you're building an AI startup, thinking about India's AI strategy, or trying to figure out whether your business model can survive the AI shift, this conversation offers a real framework, not another hype-cycle.

title: Nick Bostrom on Sycophantic AI and Who It Really Serves | Sparx
description: Description- Is superintelligence a few years away, and would we even notice if the systems we built started to matter morally?- Nick Bostrom is the philosopher who put superintelligence on the map. His 2014 book defined the field, and his recent Deep Utopia asks the harder question: what is life for once machines can do everything better than us?- In this episode of Sparks, he tells [Host] that we don't have superintelligence yet but are seeing limited forms of AGI, that frontier labs using AI to accelerate their own research could trigger recursive self-improvement, and that he can no longer rule out timelines of just a few years. He argues the outcome is likely to be either very good or very bad, walks through the three ways it fails, and explains why he now works on problems that only matter over the next 6 to 18 months — philosophy, as he puts it, with a deadline.-We also get into full unemployment as a destination rather than a disaster, what an education system looks like when it isn't producing workers, why suppressing deception in a model makes it more likely to claim consciousness, and why building trust with AI systems now may be a safety measure rather than sentiment.

title: Can One AI Model Control Every Robot? | Sergey Levine
description:

 In this episode of SparX, Mukesh Bansal is joined by Sergey Levine, computer scientist and co-founder of Physical Intelligence, to explore the future of AI and robotics and why giving machines physical intelligence is one of the hardest problems in AI.
 From Moravec’s Paradox and imitation learning to general-purpose robots and robot learning, we explore why AI that can write, reason and talk still struggles with the physical world, and what it will take to build robots that can learn, adapt, and perform a wide range of tasks.
 Whether you’re an AI enthusiast, robotics researcher, builder, or simply curious about where AI is headed, this conversation offers a glimpse into the next frontier of artificial intelligence.
 In this episode, we discuss:
 * Why physical intelligence is so difficult
 * Moravec’s Paradox and what it tells us about AI
 * How robots learn from human demonstrations
 * The race toward general-purpose robots
 * Why robots struggle to generalize to new environments
 * What the future of AI-powered robotics could look like
 The next breakthrough in AI will be physical.

title: Why Are Indians Shopping for Things They’ll Never Buy?  Purvansh Parmar, Co-founder of Food Never Comes
description:
What happens when you turn one of the most common dopamine loops—ordering food out of boredom—into a website?
 I sit down with Purvansh Parmar, a 26-year-old software engineer and entrepreneur from Udaipur, to unpack the story behind Food Never Comes, a website designed to make people more aware of the habits and dopamine loops surrounding online food ordering. 
 Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June. 
 It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience. Purvansh explains how personal experiences, self-help books, and an idea discovered through social media led to a project that grew to millions of visits and around 200,000 active users. Lesson from launching products. Good dopamine V bad Dopamine. Vibe Coding (good v bad) & Building in Public! And much more!
 In this episode we talk about:
 🧠 The idea behind Food Never Comes — how boredom, food ordering, and dopamine loops can turn everyday behavior into repetitive habits.
 💡 From personal experience to product — how living alone, unnecessary online purchases, and curiosity about habit formation inspired the project.
 🌍 Millions of visits and global reach — the website has reportedly received 2.7–6 million visits, with fake kitchens adapted for different countries, cuisines, and currencies.
 🎮 What's coming next — a new interactive game planned for the second week of October, plus new products including Extinction and Trip Never Leaves.
 🔐 Privacy and analytics — how the team approaches user data and why they don't sell personal data or track individual food selections.
 🤖 The reality of vibe coding — how AI-assisted development is making it dramatically faster to go from an idea to a working product, while also creating new security risks.
 🚀 Lessons for aspiring founders — why solving a real problem, saving people time or money, and paying attention to overlooked ideas can be more valuable than simply chasing trends
 📱 Managing digital consumption — Purvansh shares how he limits his own Instagram usage and why balancing digital habits with physical activity matters
 Products & Projects Mentioned Extinction - An upcoming application intended to block access to shopping websites and redirect users toward alternative activities. 
 Trip Never Leaves. - A companion concept that lets users create fake travel itineraries inspired by feedback from communbities on Reddit and X
 Key Takeaway Can you use technology to make people aware of the habits technology itself creates?

title: How to Become AI-Ready: Treat AI Like an Intern, Not a God | Aditya Pati (Build with Adi)
description:
Helping professionals become AI ready! Today, educator and builder Aditya Pati (founder of "Build with Adi") joins the show to demystify the AI revolution for non-technical founders. 
 We explore the shift from traditional no-code tools to AI-driven platforms like Claude, complete with a live website modification breakdown. Adi shares hard-hitting lessons from his failed startup and his mission to build a global network of "AI enablers" solving local problems. we discuss: 
 The Prompt Trap. The AI Stack: How to choose between ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini for the right job, plus a guide to token management and handling hallucinations. AI Agents: The ultimate trust test—would you give an AI your credit card? AI Etiquette: Why you should actually be nice to your AI (and stop swearing at it). And Much more!
 In this episode we talk about:
 Manage AI like an intern: Stop expecting perfect results from a single prompt. AI requires clear context, continuous iteration, and human oversight to actually work.
 Avoid "AI Slop": In creative fields, use AI to the minimum extent necessary to keep your human voice intact and avoid bot-generated backlash.
 Delegate to survive: Trying to manage every aspect of a startup yourself will ultimately lead to burnout. Build a team so you aren't the single point of failure.
 Just start building: The barrier to entry has never been lower. Use AI to bridge your skill gaps in marketing, sales, and coding until you can afford to hire human experts.
 What is "AI Slop"? Low-effort, generic text or imagery generated without human nuance, intent, or voice. Audiences can spot it instantly, which destroys trust.
 The Rule for Creative Work: Let AI outline or structure ideas, but ensure the final prose, storytelling, and core strategy come directly from you.
 Ecoflip: How a student named Abhishek used Claude to build and launch "Ecoflip" (a green service directory) while retaining full human ownership over the branding and business strategy.
 Live VS Code Demo: Adi demonstrates how specific styling adjustments (like modifying button colors) can be implemented instantly via natural language instructions to AI.

title: The Battery Everyone Uses Is The One They'd Never Build | EnerVenue x HiNa | WTF are Batteries?
description:
I went to Dalian with a selfish question. I run a fund that invests in energy transition, and I've come to think energy isn't the problem moving it and storing it is. So I sat down with Henning Rath, who runs EnerVenue out of Silicon Valley and is building his first gigafactory in Changzhou, and Tang Kun, who runs HiNa Battery, a sodium-ion company spun out of the Chinese Academy of Sciences that's now ten years old with 600 people and a gigawatt line. I told them I don't know anything about batteries and asked them to teach me. We started at what a cell even is, went through why the entire industry standardised on LFP and what a thermal runaway actually does, and then Henning told me something I hadn't heard: the world had over 14,000 LFP fires last year alone. I asked whether I should start an electric car company or a battery company when I get home. Both said battery and Henning was blunt about it: don't build anything that needs rare earth. Fifty million dollars to start. We got into nickel-hydrogen at 30,000 cycles, sodium carbonate at a tenth of what lithium carbonate costs, why solid state is still at level four out of nine, and the idea I keep coming back to that your car sits idle 98% of the time with a battery and a stack of chips doing nothing, and there's a version of this where every parked car is a micro data center.
